title: Heaven on earth
hook: the Orthodox see the Divine Liturgy as joining heaven's worship now

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cherubic Hymn. Your line was lay aside all cares. What did you set down at a door, and did it feel different picking it back up? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

An old Russian chronicle tells of envoys sent by a prince of Kiev to Constantinople. They're led into the great church there while the Liturgy is being sung. Chant, lamps, incense, a dome overhead. When they get home, they struggle to describe it. The chronicle gives their report, in substance: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people, and we can't forget that beauty. Whatever historians make of the story, it's a striking thing to say about a church service. It's our last stop on the Orthodox way of the heart, and today's word: heaven on earth.

For Orthodox Christians, that line isn't only a traveler's compliment. It's close to how their church describes the Divine Liturgy itself. Not a play about heaven. Not a memory of heaven. A joining in, now, with worship that's already going on there. The Bible gives them the picture. In Revelation, John is shown the throne of God, and creatures around it who "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." A song with no gaps in it. The Liturgy steps into that song for a while. Then the letter to the Hebrews tells ordinary believers: "ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels." Ye are come. Not, you'll get there someday. The church building says it too. The saints on the icons stand with the people, so the room is never only as full as it looks. Incense goes up, and Revelation has that picture as well: the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rising before God. That's why yesterday's hymn asked everyone to lay their cares aside. You're about to stand in a crowded room. Look back across this week and you can see the whole road: guarding the door of the heart, tears that wash, a knot for each prayer, an elder to help you hear, a mountain at prayer, cares set down. It all leads here, to the plain claim the Orthodox make about their worship: heaven is not far off. It's near.

Here's the practice: worship as if heaven were near. Sit, and breathe. Let the room around you grow larger in your mind. Not empty: full. If you pray, you can say the line from Revelation, holy, holy, holy, and let it join a song the text says never stops. If you don't pray, simply sit as if you were in very good company, unhurried, unseen, and not alone. The bell holds the time.
Heaven on earth. The Orthodox picture of the Divine Liturgy: not watching heaven from far away, but joining its worship now.

Your line: heaven is near. Today, at one ordinary spot, a sink, a bus stop, a doorway, pause and act as if the room were full. Tomorrow we open a new room in the house: Francis of Assisi. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians gather for the Divine Liturgy on Sundays and feasts; with icons, incense and chant, the service is understood as a sharing in the worship of heaven, and it leads to communion.

notes: The Primary Chronicle's envoy story is paraphrased; the prince (Vladimir) is not named and no date is given. In the chronicle the envoys also visit other peoples' worship; that part is deliberately left out so no tradition is ranked. Confirm the framing.
'Whatever else is legend in that chronicle' signals that historians treat the episode cautiously; confirm the tone.

Week-end look back: watchfulness (1121), tears (1122), prayer rope (1123), elder (1124), Athos (1125), Cherubic Hymn (1126). Also the last day of 'The Orthodox way of the heart'; the carry points to the Franciscans.
'The saints on the icons stand with the people' and incense echoing Revelation 8:4 are given as how the church building is read; confirm.
Pronunciation of Θεία Λειτουργία in modern Greek style; confirm.
